author: Ryan Blessing Sun staff writer
title: Westerly wastewater upgrades start, with state financing in place | Daily-news-alerts | thewesterlysun.com
text:
WESTERLY — A state agency has approved the first $45 million loan that will finance more than half of Westerly's massive planned upgrade to its wastewater treatment facility in the coming years.
The Rhode Island Infrastructure Bank announced Wednesday it has closed Clean Water State Revolving Fund loan to the town. The loan is the first phase of an $85 million project to modernize and upgrade the town’s wastewater treatment infrastructure.
“Wastewater infrastructure is something that people often take for granted, but it is essential to our communities, and to protecting public health and the environment” Rhode Island Infrastructure Bank Executive Director William Fazioli said. “This $45 million Clean Water State Revolving Fund loan provides Westerly with the low-cost financing needed to undertake these critical wastewater treatment system upgrades,"
By getting a 20-year loan with a 2.85% interest rate through the Infrastructure Bank, Westerly ratepayers will save more than $6 million in interest payments compared to a market-rate loan, Fazioli said.
"This is a vivid example of the Infrastructure Bank’s financial model providing direct relief to our clients during a time of rising interest rates," he said. "We are pleased to partner with the town on the first phase of a project that will ensure their wastewater system remains efficient and reliable for decades to come.”
The town's borrowing from the Infrastructure Bank for the work comes in two 20-year loans: the initial, approved $45 million draw now, followed by the second $40 million two to three years later as the project has progressed and more funds are necessary.
The project began on July 6, Town Manager Shawn Lacey said, with the town in possession of a state Department of Environmental Management certificate of approval.
Almost every area of the plant will be affected. Key improvements in Phase I include the rehabilitation of the headworks building and odor control system, primary and secondary clarifiers, and existing aeration tanks. The project also features a completely new electrical system, flood resiliency improvements, efforts to bring the facility to a state of good repair and the major treatment work to meet lower nitrogen effluent limits. Among the new installation at the plant would be aeration basins and a pump station, chemical storage and feed systems, high-flow piping, an emergency generator, building roof replacements and HVAC systems.
The plant is responsible for between 3.3 million and 4 million gallons per day of wastewater. The processed, clean water — that is minus the sewage — goes into the Pawcatuck River.
Lacey said the upgrades are essential for the community’s long-term health and growth, and to protecting the environment.
"This first phase of modernization at our wastewater treatment facility is a big undertaking," he said. "We thank the Rhode Island Infrastructure Bank for providing the financing to move this project forward, and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management for helping us navigate the regulatory permitting process.”
DEM Director Terry Gray said the work will strengthen the reliability, resilience and performance of a vital public service while protecting the health of the surrounding environment.
"Modernizing Westerly’s treatment facility will ensure the town has the infrastructure needed to meet both current and future wastewater treatment demands, while advancing efforts to improve water quality and protect Rhode Island’s valuable natural resources," Gray said.
In April, the town hired the Jacobs Project Management Company to oversee the project. Jacobs' proposal and quote for the work came in at $83.3 million, or $1.7 million less than the council has authorized in total for expenditures on the far-ranging project.
It was back in February that the council approved a payment plan where users of the sewer system would pay a $400 annual flat fee in 2027 and 2028 that would rise to $450 the subsequent three years. Their sewer tax rate would start at $1.08 per $1,000 of assessed value and top out a few years later at $1.54 per $1,000.
Non-users would see a sewer assessment of 15 cents per $1,000 of assessed value for the years 2027 and 2028, which would rise to 25 cents for the three subsequent years.
The projected “all-in” cost for a homeowner with property not in the sewer district and valued at $600,000 would be $312 annually, from 2031 to 2036. For a sewer user, the “all-in” cost on a similar home would be $779 annually. That does not include the $400 user fee.
The financing will be through revenue bonds, meaning they would not be backed by the town’s “full faith and credit,” its credit rating, but by the sewer fees and tax and the general fund, a 50-50 split.
Westerly's long-planned wastewater upgrades have been a tale of slowly mounting costs. According to Lacey in February, the DEM negotiated changes that brought the work down from close to $100 million.
A 2021 consent agreement between the town and DEM resulted in the production of an approved facility plan update in early 2024, and the DEM order of approval in August of 2025. Under the consent agreement, the construction of improvements would be complete by Jan. 20, 2029.
A key goal of the work is the lowering of the facility’s nitrogen and ammonia limits. Currently, nitrogen is limited to 15 milligrams per liter and ammonia 5.5 milligrams per liter. Those would drop to 5 mg per liter and 1.7 mg per liter, respectively.

The project also features a completely new electrical system, flood resiliency improvements, efforts to bring the facility to a state of good repair and the major treatment work to meet lower nitrogen effluent limits.
